name: Grey teal
lede: Grey teal is a muted, greyed blue-green named for the teal duck's head feathers, carried by Ridgway in 1912 and the ISCC-NBS system in 1955, and painted most often by Eugène Boudin among the artists in our archive.

sections.title: A duck's feather, greyed
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* records this hue, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 filed it as a light greenish blue [1]. Teal takes its name from the teal duck, whose iridescent head patch gives the bright original; this name mutes that patch toward grey [2]. In Munsell terms it sits near 1.6B 6.5/2.8: pale, low chroma, tipped slightly blue of pure green-blue [2].

The nearest named color is [[pastel-turquoise|Pastel Turquoise]], 3.9 units away and almost the same; [[greenish-blue|Greenish Blue]] sits at 4.0, darker [2]. The library also carries Dark Pastel Turquoise and Glaucous-Blue as near-duplicate names for the same small patch of color [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Grey teal appears in 243 of our 23,781 paintings, as photographed, more common than 66 percent of the archive's named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, at 2.1 times the expected rate, and Eugène Boudin carries it most often, in 4 of his 33 works here, though no painter stands out sharply against the museum baseline [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color [3]. The earliest match is dated 1375, 537 years before Ridgway's 1912 record — a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof of any teal-named pigment, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3].
